title: Invert Binary Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting nodes then swapping separately versus a single recursive invert-and-swap pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree (swap every node's left and right children, recursively throughout) and return its root.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Inverting a tree means recursively inverting the left and right subtrees, then swapping which side they attach to on the current node. A leaf node (or empty node) is unaffected, since it has no children to swap.

blocks.title: Analogy: Flipping a Family Tree Left to Right
blocks.text: Picture a family tree chart, flipped left-to-right like a mirror image: every branching point has its left and right branches swapped, all the way down.

blocks.caption: Invert both subtrees first, then swap them onto the current node

blocks.text: Inverted preorder: 4 7 9 null null 6 null null 2 3 null null 1 null null.
Inverted preorder: 2 3 null null 1 null null.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An empty tree inverts to itself (still empty).

Observation 2: Inverting a node means the left subtree and right subtree must each be inverted individually, THEN attached to the OPPOSITE side of the current node.

Observation 3: This recursive definition applies uniformly at every level, so a single recursive function handles the entire tree.
This leads to a direct recursive function: invert both children first, then swap them onto the current node.
Conceptually, collect all nodes via any traversal first, then make a separate pass swapping each node's children.
Why the code is written this way

items: Collecting nodes first, then swapping in a second pass, implements the definition in two clearly separated steps.
This uses unnecessary O(n) extra space for the node list, when a single recursive pass achieves the same result directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text: Time: O(n). Space: O(n) for the node list.
Limitation: a single recursive function inverting and swapping in one pass avoids the extra node list entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define invert(node) recursively: if node is null, return null. Otherwise, recursively invert the left subtree and the right subtree, then assign the ORIGINAL left child slot to hold the inverted RIGHT subtree, and the original right child slot to hold the inverted LEFT subtree. Return the node itself.
Use a single recursive pass: invert both children, then swap them directly onto the current node.
Dry run for root = 4, left = 2, right = 7

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["Recursively invert subtree rooted at 2","Swaps 2's children (1 and 3)"],["Recursively invert subtree rooted at 7","Swaps 7's children (6 and 9)"],["Swap onto root 4","Left becomes the inverted 7-subtree, right becomes the inverted 2-subtree"]]}

codes.python:
def invert_tree(root):
    if root is None:
        return None
    left = invert_tree(root.left)                       # invert left subtree first
    right = invert_tree(root.right)                      # invert right subtree first
    root.left, root.right = right, left                  # swap them onto this node
    return root

blocks.text: Since inverting a subtree is fully self-contained (it only rearranges nodes within that subtree), recursively inverting both children first and then swapping their positions on the parent correctly produces the mirror image at every level, all the way up to the root, in one single pass.

blocks.text: Invert Binary Tree is a canonical, minimal recursive tree problem: recurse on children, then combine (swap) their results onto the parent.

items: Swapping the children BEFORE recursing into them (using the wrong, already-swapped children in the recursive calls).
Forgetting the base case for a null node.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Empty tree","Returns null unchanged."],["Single node tree","Returns the same single node unchanged (no children to swap)."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "invert each subtree first, then swap their positions on the parent" clarifies the exact order of operations needed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "mirror a binary tree", think: recursively invert children, then swap them onto the current node.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches visit every node once, O(n); the direct recursive swap avoids the brute force's extra O(n) space for a node list.

items: Pattern: recurse on children, then combine (swap) their results onto the parent.
Core Idea: invert both subtrees first, then swap their positions on the current node.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's node list, O(h) recursion depth for the direct approach.
Most Important Observation: recursing before swapping (not after) uses the correctly inverted subtrees.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, easy recursive tree problem.
One line memory trick: invert both sides, then swap them.
